If the well is off-center in a bounded reservoir, the distances to the surrounding boundaries are different. Because pressure disturbances propagate outward from the well, the **closest boundary is reached first**, so its effect appears earlier and more strongly than the effect of farther boundaries. That is why boundary effects can arrive **unevenly** in time and magnitude.

An **image well** is a mathematical way to represent a boundary by placing a fictitious well on the opposite side of the boundary at the same perpendicular distance from it as the real well. For a **sealing (no-flow) boundary**, the image well has the **same rate and same sign** as the producing well, so the boundary condition of zero normal flow is satisfied. In practice, if the nearest boundary is the one that dominates early-time behavior, a single image well placed symmetrically across that boundary can approximate its effect.

If you want, I can also sketch how this differs for a constant-pressure boundary versus a no-flow boundary.
